Hi Priyom,

Thanks for taking this on. As part of our SIG review we need a concise packet describing how Redwood proposes to handle network connectivity between MedCore's VPCs and Redwood Private (VPC peer or private endpoint), and the set of egress IPs we should allow on our side. Specifically we need:

- A short diagram showing peering vs private endpoint choice (PDF)
- Confirmed egress IPs (or ranges) for outbound traffic from Redwood to MedCore APIs (for allowlist)
- Whether traffic will originate from NAT gateway IP(s) or service-managed static IPs
- A short list of steps and expected timelines to complete peering and firewall changes

Also include any supporting evidence for network controls (screenshots of peering acceptance, NAT config, or the signed peering agreement). Our procurement team will want an ATO window — can you flag any maintenance / expected disruption?

Ideally we need the packet by EOD Jul 21. If there are blockers, let me know earlier.

Thanks,
Asha Rao
Security & Compliance
MedCore Health

Hi Asha — appreciate the clear list. Laura (cc) and I coordinated with infra; summary below and we'll attach a diagram (redwood_vpc_peering_diagram.pdf) and a zip with evidence. Short answers up front:

- Connectivity model: VPC Peering (primary) with option for AWS PrivateLink (private endpoint) on request. We recommend Peering for lower latency; PrivateLink available if you need private IPs on your side only.
- Egress IPs: outbound egress to MedCore APIs will come from a small set of static NAT egress IPs per-region (see list below).
- Origin of traffic: service will egress via managed NAT gateways that we allocate per-customer install; these NAT IPs are stable for the lifetime of a Dedicated/Private deployment and will be provided in the evidence zip.
- Timeline: peering setup + routing changes typically 1–2 business days once you accept the peering connection; firewall changes on your side depend on change window. No planned disruption to production during setup if routes are added as non-destructive.

Egress IP ranges (us-west-2):
- 34.210.45.17/32
- 34.210.45.18/32
- 54.152.200.128/26

We've attached: redwood_vpc_peering_diagram.pdf and sig-network-evidence.zip (contains screenshots of peering request, NAT allocation, and a sample peering acceptance email).

Next steps: can you confirm the AWS account ID we'll peer with and whether you prefer Peering or PrivateLink? Once you confirm, I'll open the peering request and share the Jira link for tracking.

Thanks,
Priyom Das
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Thanks, Priyom — that helps. A couple of clarifications:

1) Our security team requires a dedicated set of egress IPs that do not change for the course of the contract. The /32s you listed are fine, but can you confirm they are reserved specifically for MedCore (i.e., not shared across other customers)?

2) On the peering vs PrivateLink point: we typically prefer PrivateLink for production (less blast radius) but have an approval path for peering if latency or cross-account access is required. If you support PrivateLink, please include port and DNS mapping guidance.

3) Please include any evidence that these NAT IPs are preserved across infra restarts and not ephemeral. A short screenshot of the named allocation in our account or a support ticket would be ideal.

We will provide you the AWS account ID by EOD Jul 20. Procurement will review the peering agreement after we confirm the model.

Best,
Asha

Hi Asha — looping in the infra owner for the technical confirmations. Answers below (short + bullets):

- Dedicated IPs: Confirmed. The three /32 addresses listed earlier are reserved in our customer allocation pool and will be dedicated to the MedCore Private deployment once the peering request is accepted; they are not used for other tenants. Evidence: see sig-network-evidence.zip -> nat_allocations/medcore_named_alloc.png (screenshot of allocation with tag medcore-prod).

- Persistence: NAT allocation is tied to an Elastic IP allocation backed by our infra provisioning service. It will survive instance restarts and is only released if explicitly decommissioned by engineering (documented SOP). Evidence includes a support ticket stub and the SOP excerpt.

- PrivateLink details (if you choose):
  - Ports: TCP 443 (HTTPS) endpoints by default; additional ports can be opened on request
  - DNS: We publish a private hosted zone in your account with the endpoint DNS name; sample mapping included in evidence zip.
  - TLDR: PrivateLink works but requires you to create the VPC endpoint and accept the service name on your side; we'll provide Terraform snippets to automate this.

- Peering steps (high level):
  1) MedCore sends AWS Account ID and VPC ID to Redwood.
  2) Redwood opens Peering Connection request and shares request ID.
  3) MedCore accepts peering in their console and adds route entries for Redwood CIDRs.
  4) Redwood validates routes and flips traffic. No service downtime expected.

Tracking & paperwork:
- Jira: NET-4821 (peering acceptance and validation)
- Confluence: Integration notes linked above
- DocuSign: Peering agreement draft at https://app.docusign.com/peering/medcore-agreement-789

Let us know the account ID and preferred model (Peering or PrivateLink) and we will open the request immediately.

Cheers,
Karthik Iyer
Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
